newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Nations issue stamps for children of Chernobyl.
newsitem.headline: Nations issue stamps for children of Chernobyl.

text.p: Some 20 countries issued stamps in a philatelic effort to commemorate the 1986 Chernobyl nuclear disaster that unleashed a lethal radioactive cloud over Europe, blighting millions of lives.
Actor Jon Voigt and Nobel laureate Elie Wiesel led a gala ceremony on Monday evening sponsored by the Chabad Children of Chernobyl and the U.N. Educational, Social and Cultural Organisation (UNESCO).

The stamps will be marketed to collectors by the International Government Philatelic Corporation, the world's largest company of its kind, in an effort to raise funds for future Chernobyl relief efforts.
UNESCO has helped establish nine humanitarian aid centres in the Ukraine, Belarus and western Russia to help people whose lives have been disrupted by the disaster.

Chabad, an ultra-religious Chassidic group, which organised the philatelic effort, has brought 1,442 Jewish children to Israel on 28 flights over the past six year. It has shipped food and medical supplies and trained medical professional to people in contaminated areas.

Those issuing the stamps included Antigua, Armenia, Belarus, Bhutan, Dominica, Gambia, Ghana, Grenada Guyana, India, Jamaica, Liberia, Norfold Islands, Philippines, Sierre Leone, South Africa, St Vincent, Tanzania, Uganda and Zambia.

Many of the children are suffering from an enlarged thyroid, respiratory diseases and in all cases nausea and weakness attributed to the nuclear disaster, according to testimony at the ceremony. In most cases their parents immigrate to Israel.

According to the World Health Organisation, thyroid cancer is expected to escalate dramatically a decade after the Chernobyl disaster, which occurred in April 1986. For unexplained reasons Jews are at least three times more suspectible to thyroid cancer than non-Jews.

The Ukraine says 4,300 people died as a direct result of the accident and many of its 350,000 clean-up workers are now ill. Millions were affected, mostly in Ukraine, western Russia and Belarus, which was downwind from the blast and worst hit.
